I graduated with Biology last September, but lacking the passion in the field I decided to take some Coding School and eventually got a job in Front End Web Development. However I want to eventually make my way back to field of science, but this time my major of choice is Chemical Engineering, where I want to work on plastic decomposition and carbon sequestration, but I have several barriers. 1) Mediocre grades - I barely pulled an 2.8 because of depression from family situation. 2) Lack of practical lab experience- I have some, but none relevant to Chemistry 3) Have no Chemistry related upper div courses - another school rejected me from Chemistry graduate program because of this 4) Lack of real connections- I have not gotten to know professors at my school really well, and it becomes harder to ask as I graduated September of last year.

I hope to apply some time next year, but I need to hit the books and the papers. Furthermore, how can I ameliorate above mentioned problems where I can be a serious contender for Graduate program?
How should I get ready for graduate school again?

A good first step would be to nail the GRE. Both the general and subject tests. You can actually learn chemistry on your own, and if you put the smack down on the chemistry GRE it's proof that you're ready, whether you have the coursework background or not. A pair of really hot scores will be tangible proof of what you're capable of that you can set on somebody's desk and that they can take in at one glance. Of course, this is no magic bullet - it's going to depend on you investing huge time and effort into actually learning chemistry. But then again, that's what graduate school is all about.
What about recommendation letters? I don't have many professors that I feel comfortable enough to ask.

Grow a pair and ask anyway. If they turn you down, smile politely, say you understand, and walk away, and you are none the worse for wear. They get requests like this all the time, and some have a template they use where they just have to change names and dates. Others are more picky. But you have to keep in mind that you have nothing to lose by asking, other than the temporary and minor embarrassment of being turned down.

I think the GRE is a good idea, as Moonbat said. Every school uses GRE scores differently, but a solid GRE subject test score will only help you. Just a word of warning - the general test is pretty easy, but the subject tests can be difficult. If you wind up taking them, don't let the easiness of the general test give you a false sense of how the subject test will go. Remember - a lot of non-native English speakers and non-science people are taking this test too, so this is your competition. The same is not true for the subject tests. Study your ass off, and take the subject test seriously. (Disclaimer: This is how it was when I took them ~10 years ago, and I took the Biochemistry test, not Chemistry. Might be a good idea to find people with recent experience with that particular test.)

I'll be honest - I see two big problems here regarding your lack of experience. You hit on one of them - you're going to have an uphill battle applying to chemistry programs without a lot of chemistry experience. The second problem - are you sure this is what you want? The attrition rate in PhD programs is pretty high, and a lot of people that graduate eventually leave science because it wasn't what they thought it would be. I think it would be good for you (personally and professionally) to have some research experience before you sign away your life for the next 5-10 years. You said you had some lab experience, but specifically what was it? Just the usual undergraduate lab courses, or actual research in a lab? Can you go into more detail there? If you want to know how to get experience in chemical engineering, I can't help you there. Not my field. Maybe a master's program? Is there some sort of entry-level chemical engineering job you could get? One suggestion that I'll add here is to think outside the box a little, and don't focus your search on just chemistry programs. With your background, it might be easier to get into a biology/biochemistry program, and there's so much overlap between fields of science, that you might be able to find some chemistry-leaning labs in programs like these. Even something like synthetic biology might work for you. It's possible that you might just not have liked whatever particular flavor of biology you were doing before. It's going to take a lot of work on your part to find these labs and what programs they're in, but this is something that prospective grad students should be doing anyway.

Lab experiences I had were:

undergraduate courses

upper div requirements - Plant lab, and Field Biology lab

and Synthetic Biology Club - I decided to quit because I felt the need to focus on my classes.

Thanks. Unfortunately, it's gonna be tough to go directly to where you want to be with that sort of lab experience. I'm not saying it's impossible, but it's a big negative for you. Does that mean you're incapable of succeeding in a grad program? No, of course not. It just means you're going to have a harder time being noticed and taken seriously by the admissions committee, so don't take the rejection personally. I think the best thing you can do is get some experience before you go to grad school - look for an entry-level job for a year or two, maybe a master's or a post-bac program. Something to establish a track record of success in your field (and to see if you like it). If you're really committed to going straight to grad school, you might also want to try contacting professors directly to see what they would recommend doing. Most probably won't respond (that's normal... be persistent, but not too persistent), but you might be able to spark up a conversation with one of them and who knows where that could lead... Maybe they're looking for a research assistant? Maybe they'll see something they like in you and push the admissions committee to accept you? Just gotta put yourself out there, get noticed, be respectful, and leverage the skills you do have.

Analytical chemist here, don't expect this to be very accurate. It will probably be able to tell you if that eight ball you bought contains cocaine, but don't think that the percent purity it gives you is in any way accurate. It probably won't even be able to detect residual pesticides in produce. Laboratory grade spectrometers are big and expensive for a reason.
Lab grade usually cost millions for a reason
It's not millions, a uv-vis analytical spectrometer is about $25k, there are very few spectrometers that cost more than $100k.
Huh. It's always weird to realize how good of a research insitution you attend based on factors like the cost of your lab's spec machines.

Oh yeah, for sure. The gold standard of research institution instrumentation is the Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectrometer (NMR) also known as the MRI. These are very expensive and require regular addition of liquid helium and nitrogen, which also isn't cheap. NMR spectrometers are measured by resolution, the higher the resolution, the more expensive the model. Sometimes these things are huge and take up entire rooms with their magnetic fields. Look a few up if you're curious, but they're definitely the quickest way to judge a research institution.
